newsitem.title: USA: Richmond Fed says local labor mart unusually tight.
newsitem.headline: Richmond Fed says local labor mart unusually tight.

text.p: The Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond has detected unusually tight labor market conditions in its region, which has been viewed as a concern by local businesses, a Richmond Fed economist said.
"I think the single biggest cause for concern here would be the unusually tight labor markets," Richmond Fed economist Raymond Owens told Reuters.
"We hear quite a few comments from businessmen, and certainly those comments indicate that exceedingly tight labor markets are their single biggest concern," Owens added.
Owens said economic growth in the region seemed to be running at a solid pace, while recent weakeness in some specific parts of the district's manufacturing sectors appeared to be nearing an end.
"In the manufacturing sector, those key components where weakness has been -- apparel, textile, and furniture -- perhaps is coming to an end now," he said.

"Layoffs appear to be trailing off in those particular manufacturing sectors ... And it does appear that these manufacturing sectors are perhaps headed for a brighter future than they've experienced," he added.
The economist said the phenomenon was particularly apparent in North and South Carolina.
The Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond covers the country's fifth economic region, which includes the District of Columbia, Maryland, North Carolina, South Carolina, Virginia and most of West Virginia.
Owens also said some isolated wage pressures seemed to be on the horizon. "We do look at some pressures perhaps isolated at this point of rising wages," the Richmond Fed economist said.

He said it was still hard to tell whether the incipient signs of wage pressures would lead to a pick up in wages in the near future, but he stressed that "certainly (labor) markets in our district do remain quite tight."

The economist added that the Richmond Fed had received numerous comments from local employers, saying wages have been moving up, particularly for two groups -- highly skilled workers, especially those with computer knowledge, and also unskilled workers.
